papers.title: No allocentric distractor-location learning following self-movement even with contextual anchors and explicit knowledge
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires learning where relevant information can likely be found, but also where distraction is likely to occur. For such learning to be useful in everyday life, it must generalize across changing viewpoints as observers move through the environment. Recent work suggests a striking asymmetry in this regard: whereas target-location learning can be grounded in world-centered coordinates, distractor-location learning appears tied to the observer’s current viewpoint. One possibility is that allocentric distractor-location learning requires stronger contextual support than allocentric target-location learning. Alternatively, distractor suppression may be fundamentally constrained by viewer-centered spatial coding. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants performed an additional-singleton search task displayed on a tabletop and continuously changed their standing position around the table, while the high-probability distractor location remained fixed in the external environment. Unlike previous studies using this paradigm, contextual anchors were embedded directly within the search display, allowing distractor locations to be encoded relative to a stable task-relevant allocentric structure. In a second experiment, participants were additionally explicitly informed about the distractor-location regularity. Despite task-relevant contextual structure and explicit knowledge, distractor-location learning failed to emerge in world-centered coordinates. Together with previous findings showing robust egocentric distractor-location learning using the same set-up, these findings strengthen the view that learned distractor suppression relies primarily on viewer-centered spatial coding, potentially reflecting a process linked to viewpoint-specific action selection.

papers.title: Contemplative mindfulness and its influence on firm service performance: a configurational analysis
papers.abstract:
This study aims to explore the implementation of contemplative mindfulness, rooted in Eastern traditions, in service-oriented firms. It examines how employees’ mindfulness practices impact key service outcomes, including service creativity performance and adaptive behavior in service offerings, which have been underexplored in prior research.
 
 
 
 This study examines 282 service firms using 565 questionnaires. It uses fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis to explore the relationship between contemplative mindfulness practices and service performance-related variables.
 
 
 
 This study reveals that a heightened presence of practices related to mind and memory, present-moment awareness and right effort is indispensable for achieving higher levels of service creativity performance. In addition, this study identifies that present-moment awareness and attention practices, along with the right effort, are necessary for facilitating adaptive behavior in service offerings. Furthermore, this study highlights that clear comprehension practices and ethical viewpoints are peripheral conditions that influence both service creativity performance and adaptive behavior in service offerings.
 
 
 
 The study’s focus on 282 firms and its specific survey methodology limit the generalizability of the findings to other industries.
 
 
 
 Firms seeking to boost service creativity and adaptability should acknowledge the crucial role of contemplative mindfulness practices practiced by employees in service settings and actively promote awareness of their numerous benefits for staff.
 
 
 
 This study adds to the existing literature on service management by going beyond Western-centric mindfulness ideas to examine contemplative mindfulness. It also creates a practical framework for applying contemplative mindfulness practices in service firms.

papers.title: Introducing interdisciplinary contemplative pedagogy: a case study of ‘The Art and Science of Meditation’
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article presents a model for the application of contemplative pedagogy in higher education, with a focus on rich contextualisation and interdisciplinarity. We articulate a vision for a multiplicity of contemplative pedagogies and present a conceptual framework to guide the understanding, analysis, and evaluation of contemplative practices within learning processes. This framework draws from a range of disciplinary perspectives, placing the embodied activity of contemplative practices in concentric layers of context. We extend the discussion of contemplative pedagogies by exploring several challenges that educators may confront in contemporary university settings. The concept of cosmopolitanism is introduced to reason through the epistemological, cultural, and practical diversity that educators and students encounter when engaging with contemplative practices as part of educational life. To illustrate how the model of contextualised, interdisciplinary contemplative pedagogies can be applied, we present ‘The Art and Science of Meditation’, a first-year undergraduate course designed by the authors.

Inner Calm: The Transformative Power of Meditation and Contemplative Practices in Stress Reduction
papers.abstract: In an increasingly fast-paced and demanding world, stress has become a common feature of modern life. From workplace pressure to personal responsibilities, individuals constantly grapple with mental and emotional strain. Amid various strategies for managing stress, meditation and contemplative practices have emerged as powerful tools. These ancient practices offer a path not only to relaxation but also to deep mental clarity and emotional balance. Stress, while a natural physiological response, can become harmful when chronic. Prolonged stress contributes to a range of health issues, including anxiety, depression, cardiovascular problems, and weakened immunity. It affects both the mind and body, disrupting sleep, concentration, and overall well-being. Therefore, effective stress management is essential for maintaining health and quality of life. Meditation is a practice that encourages focused attention, awareness, and a calm mental state. Techniques such as mindfulness meditation, transcendental meditation, and loving-kindness meditation have gained widespread popularity due to their measurable benefits. Research indicates that regular meditation reduces cortisol levels (the primary stress hormone), enhances emotional regulation, and promotes a sense of peace. Mindfulness meditation, in particular, trains individuals to observe their thoughts and emotions without judgment. This non-reactive awareness helps prevent overthinking and reduces the intensity of stressful experiences. Beyond meditation, contemplative practices like prayer, journaling, deep breathing, and nature walks also contribute to stress reduction. These practices encourage introspection and a deeper connection with oneself and the world. They help individuals slow down, reflect, and foster resilience in the face of challenges. Spiritual contemplation, regardless of religious affiliation, can also provide a sense of purpose and meaning, which acts as a buffer against stress. Numerous studies support the efficacy of meditation and contemplative practices. Neuroscientific research shows changes in brain regions related to emotion regulation, attention, and self-awareness in those who meditate regularly. These practices are also being integrated into clinical settings, schools, and workplaces as preventive and therapeutic tools. Incorporating just a few minutes of daily meditation or reflection can significantly enhance one’s ability to manage stress and maintain mental health. Meditation and contemplative practices offer more than temporary relief and they cultivate a lasting sense of inner peace and emotional strength. By promoting mindfulness, self-awareness, and compassion, they empower individuals to respond to life’s challenges with clarity and calm. In the journey toward holistic well-being, these practices are invaluable allies.

papers.title: Aristotle's Theoria in Contemplative Education
papers.abstract: This essay analyzes Pierre Hadot's reading of Aristotelian theoria in order to evaluate theoria's relevancy for the contemporary field of Contemplative Education. It emphasizes the limited engagement with theoria against a backdrop of heightened attention to mindfulness‐based practices. The essay critiques the conflation of Plato and Aristotle's appropriations of diplomatic theoria and reveals shortcomings in Hadot's attempt to characterize theoria as a spiritual exercise of self‐cultivation at the core of an Aristotelian way of life. The critique underscores the need for a clearer delineation of Plato and Aristotle's contribution to contemporary Contemplative Education and points to the possibility of a richer exploration of theoria beyond Hadot's interpretation.

papers.title: Ethnographic Dilemmas and Reflexive Thoughts of a Contemplative Jewish Anthropologist
papers.abstract: During ethnographic fieldwork, anthropologists of religion grapple with various dilemmas regarding their participation in the rituals they study. How do they make real-time decisions between full participation and observational distance? Do they manage to participate harmoniously in religious activities even during moments of doubt or questioning of their own faith? Based on my three-year fieldwork in Israeli Reform Jewish congregations, which included observations and in-depth interviews, I demonstrate how my reflexive experience which exposes my internal Jewish dialogue, shaped my patterns of participation and motivation in engaging with various rituals. This autoethnographic description illustrates that my deliberate abstention or avoidance from participation, stemming from differences in religious habitus and my anthropological research approach, enabled congregants to engage in communal activities and thereby contributed to broadening my understanding of different communal scenarios. I discovered, thus, that the vector that determines the nature of participation is a product of the researched practice – in this case, religious performances/practices. Therefore, I suggest that this methodological decision develops ethnographic honesty and loyalty on both sides, the ethnographer’s as well as the informants’.

papers.title: Decolonial Intersectionality as a Framework of Social Justice Research in International Communication: A Contemplative Discussion
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper draws attention to the topic of social justice in relation to the field of International Communication. The field, having somewhat featured inequities prevailing in the international communication order, must revisit social justice issues anew. This paper calls for a decolonial intersectionality framework to be considered in social justice research undertakings in international communication. It makes an overview of decolonial intersectionality and highlights its potential to uncover and challenge dominant narratives and Western biases that have been prevalent in the field. It also suggests that decolonial intersectionality may also posit prospects for transforming the global communication order to be more equitable and inclusive of those historically marginalized. The discussion initially overviews how issues of inequality, race, class, and gender have surfaced in the historical evolution of international communication and then presents a case for adopting the decolonial intersectionality framework to examine social justice concerns in relation to the field of international communication.

papers.title: Effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions on psychological well-being among nurses: A systematic review of randomized and non-randomized studies.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nurses frequently experience psychological well-being challenges in clinical settings, particularly related to burnout, psychological resilience, and sleep quality. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are widely implemented to address psychological well-being in nurses. While previous reviews have primarily focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), incorporating non-randomized intervention studies may provide complementary evidence from a broader range of clinical settings. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of MBIs on nurses' burnout, psychological resilience, and sleep quality. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Medline, Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, and CINAHL up to June 2025 to identify RCTs and non- randomized intervention studies addressing the values of mindfulness-based interventions in nurses. RESULTS: A total of 16 studies involving 1124 participants were included, comprising 12 parallel-group randomized controlled trials, one randomized crossover trial, and three non-randomized intervention studies. Study-level findings generally favored MBIs for burnout, psychological resilience, and sleep quality; however, the magnitude and precision of the reported effects varied across studies, and several findings were nonsignificant. Risk-of-bias assessments ranged from low to critical, and the overall certainty of evidence for all three outcomes was low. CONCLUSION: The available evidence suggests that MBIs may have beneficial effects on burnout, psychological resilience, and sleep quality among nurses; however, confidence in these findings remains limited by methodological weaknesses, risk of bias, heterogeneity across studies, and the small evidence base for some outcomes. The non-randomized studies provide complementary information on the application of MBIs in clinical nursing settings but do not strengthen causal inference. Further rigorously designed and adequately powered randomized studies are needed to clarify the magnitude and sustainability of these effects.

papers.title: The impact of mindfulness on sleep, cognitive function and athletic performance of young males migrating to the plateau.
papers.abstract: AIMS: To examine whether an 8-week mindfulness training program was associated with changes in sleep quality, cognitive function, and athletic performance in young men who migrated to high-altitude regions. METHODS: Ninety-six young male migrants were randomly assigned to an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) program (n = 48) or a no-intervention control group (n = 48). Sleep quality (PSQI), cognitive processing (P300 latency), and athletic performance (3000-m run time) were assessed before and after the intervention. RESULTS: The mindfulness group was associated with greater improvements in sleep quality (PSQI median: 7.5 to 5 vs. 8 to 8.5, P < 0.001) and cognitive processing speed (P300 latency median: 387 ms to 357 ms vs. 376.5 ms to 374.5 ms, P = 0.01) compared with controls. Exploratory analyses suggested that P300 amplitude increased in parietal and occipital regions. No significant between-group difference was observed in 3000-m run completion time (P = 0.51) or grade improvement rates (25.0% vs. 29.17%, P = 0.65). CONCLUSION: An 8-week mindfulness intervention was associated with improved sleep quality and cognitive processing speed, but no significant association was observed with athletic performance, in young male migrants to high-altitude regions. These preliminary findings suggest potential benefits of mindfulness as a non-pharmacological strategy for high-altitude health management, pending replication with active control conditions.

papers.title: Mindfulness During Exercise and Occupational Adaptability Among Nursing Students: A Cross-Sectional Study of Associations With Psychological Resilience and Career Decision Self-Efficacy.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Occupational adaptability is relevant to nursing students' preparation for career transitions. This study examined its associations with mindfulness during exercise, psychological resilience, and career decision self-efficacy within a hypothesized correlational structural model. METHODS: A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among 779 nursing students recruited through convenience sampling. Self-report measures assessed mindfulness during exercise, psychological resilience, career decision self-efficacy, and occupational adaptability. Descriptive analyses were conducted using SPSS 29.0, and the measurement and structural models were estimated using SmartPLS 4.1. Direct and statistical indirect associations were examined using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. RESULTS: Mindfulness during exercise was positively associated with psychological resilience (β = 0.606, p < 0.001), career decision self-efficacy (β = 0.712, p < 0.001), and occupational adaptability (β = 0.520, p < 0.001). Positive indirect associations with occupational adaptability were estimated through psychological resilience (β = 0.138, 95% CI [0.091, 0.196]) and career decision self-efficacy (β = 0.134, 95% CI [0.058, 0.216]). Under the hypothesized resilience-before-self-efficacy ordering, the serial indirect coefficient was 0.019 (95% CI [0.007, 0.033]). The model accounted for 71.2% of the variance in occupational adaptability. CONCLUSIONS: Mindfulness during exercise, psychological resilience, and career decision self-efficacy were associated with nursing students' perceived occupational adaptability. The indirect estimates are conditional on the specified model and do not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation. Prospective studies are needed to examine these relationships over time.
